Karl Marx and. all the great host of socialists, right down to Stalin, worked and Laboured to destroy capitalism, and now, just in a breath, according to my right hon. friend, it has been destroyed by a few brief words delivered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning).
Well, my right hon. friend should know something about the sales tax. He was present when it stood at one per cent, and within a few yearn he had raised it to six per cent. He would not go above that; he stopped there. That was the brink- of the precipice, but he was by no means so careful in regard to the tariff. Here are some of the items on which he raised the tariff. On blankets the tariff was raised from 20-45 per cent in 1930 to 44-82 per cent in 1934. I am including

The Budget-Mr. Deachman
in these figures, of course, the landing charges, sales tax and all the other things which operate to increase the price. Think of that, Mr. Speaker. Two years ago there was in Ontario a frost so keen that it killed every apple tree in the orchard of the old farm back home in Huron county, and at the same time the right hon. gentleman was raising the tariff on blankets until it was more than double the rate of previous years. On art silk the tariff was raised from 434 per cent to 86J per cent; on wool overcoats from 264 per cent to 52i per cent; on silk and wool hosiery from 26J per cent to 704 per cent. These are only samples, and remember these are tariffs and imposts levied upon goods entering this country from Great Britain. Yet my right hon. friend was filled with the idea that we might be ruined by* a paltry eight per cent sales tax. These are tariff heights indeed! Piling Pelion on Ossa, Everest on Aconcagua, and when he had reached these heights he gazed upward and wept because there were no further tariff heights to scale.
Then we have the dear old balance of trade. No, there is another one of which I would like to speak. There is the question of magazines. I want to quote the words of my right hon. friend on that, because they are very interesting, a wonderful sentence:
Is it just or fair that the Canadian people, as a whole, should be called upon to pay half the amount of the tax that is received from one who buys this paper outside Canada rather than in it?
That is a bit confused, I am not sure what that means. Here it is:
Is it just and right and fair that on a certain type of paper brought into the dominion for a certain specific purpose there should be a rebate of fifty per cent of the duty paid, and that we should ask the taxpayers of Canada to pay the balance? Is that right?
Now, when there is a reduction in duty the consumer does not pay it, he gets paid. That is what happens in this case; there was a reduction in the duty levied upon paper, and the Canadian consumer will get his dividend- I was going to say national dividend-out of the higher quality of the magazines produced.
What	is	the brief	history of this industry? Simply this, that some years ago the magazine publishers of this country wanted	a	tariff, but	later	Mr. Fielding,instead	of	putting a	tariff	on magazines,because	he	protested against	the idea of a
tariff against thought, gave a drawback on the duties levied upon paper. In 1931, after duties had been imposed upon magazines or upon the advertising content, the Publishers' Association of Canada and the Agricultural
Press Association of Canada wrote to the leader of the government of that day and said:
The money paid by Canadian publishers in higher costs of materials and equipment should be available to them for use in increasing the effectiveness and number of their editorial pages. Canadian readers compare Canadian periodicals with all others and it is only by the production of publications of superior quality Canadian publishers can win and hold the interest of the Canadian people. If our publishers are compelled to surrender their revenues for unwarranted costs of materials and equipment they are prevented from making their editorial pages as good as foreign competition demands.
What does that mean? The publishers wanted the opportunity to develop in Canada a kind and style of publication which in appearance and editorial content would be equal to the best American papers, and what they asked of the government of that day was that paper, ink, engravings, art work, machinery and supplies used in production should have the duties reduced to a lower basis. They said:
Given an even chance in cost of production Canadian publishers are able and willing to meet all competitors.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Might I ask the hon.
gentleman from what he is reading?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am reading from a
letter sent by the Magazine Publishers' Association of Canada and the Agricultural Press Association of Canada to the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, Prime Minister and Minister of Finance, dated January 16, 1931, and I shall be very glad to let my hon. friend have the full text. It continues:
If, in the national interest, it is considered advisable to lessen the forces of foreign literature in Canada, a growing benefit, over a period of years, will accrue to Canadian publishers.
And then this underlined sentence:
But the solution of their pressing difficulties in the production of publications which will compare with all others lies in lower editorial and mechanical costs.
That is what they asked. They asked for what is given to other manufacturers, a chance to reduce the cost of their product so that they could compete fairly with American publications. They did not from that date until this ask for a duty upon magazines. Now that the Minister of Finance has done something for the magazine industry I predict that it will go forward with increasing prosperity just as it did in the days of Mr. Fielding. I have under my hand an item which shows what they did accomplish in that time. When the drawback came into effect eight leading maga-
The Budget-Mr. Deachman

zines were using 1,912 tons of paper per annum. At the time the drawback was cancelled in 1930 these publications required 5,283 tons per annum, an increase of 3,371 tons, indicating greater progress in eighteen months than had1 taken place in the previous ten years. I predict greater progress in the magazine publishing business in Canada in the next two years than has taken place in the last five under high protection.
Now a word about this ever-recurring question of the balance of trade. My right hon. friend the leader of the opposition, speaking in regard to it the other day, stated that too much emphasis had been given to it in the past. To-day I attack this general fallacy of the balance of trade on the ground that as far as Canada is concerned an increase in tariff is not conducive to a favourable balance of trade. Personally I care little whether the balance of trade is favourable or unfavourable. There have been times when we have been prosperous with an unfavourable balance; there are other nations which have been prosperous for generations with an unfavourable balance; also the reverse has been true. But I say that a high tariff policy is not conducive to a favourable balance of trade, and I prove it from Canadian history. Between 1878 and 1896 there were only five years in which there was a favourable trade balance; that is the time when protection was in flower and was guided by the master hand of Sir John A. Macdonald. During all the years of Canadian history, leaving out the war years and the immediate post-war years, the high favourable balances have been in times of low tariff and the unfavourable balances in times of high tariff. And may I point out-I am sorry that the leader of the opposition is not in his place, for I know he would agree- that in the years 1912,	1913, 1914, the
adverse trade balance of Canada was larger in proportion to total trade than ever before, especially the balance with the United States, and what was happening then? My right hon. friend was in the house and he had not one word to say because at that time the Tory flag flew at the masthead and all was right with the world.
Now what is the problem before us? ? It is simply this: Are we to go forward under low tariffs, giving a chance for expansion and development, or go back to stagnation under high tariffs? I have no hesitancy as to which course we are going to follow. If you examine the history of all the depressions of the past what do you find? The nations moved out of these depressions when tariffs were lowered and trade expanded, or when there came into

the situation some new factor which produced exactly the same result as an expansion of trade. In England one of the greatest world depressions followed the Napoleonic wars. Great Britain was not clear of that until 1846, the time of the repeal of the corn laws, but in the next ten years British trade made more progress than from the days of the invasion by Caesar until then. Why? Not only because of free trade but because about that time there came the industrial expansion which meant the development of England. Take the United States following the civil war; what happened? They passed through a depression; then came the opening of the west and the expansion by that means of the free trade area, and the United States moved forward into a great period of expansion because of the same basic cause; the free trade area of the country was expanded. Coming to our own country in 1896 what had we? Sir Wilfrid Laurier expanded trade by the adoption of the British preference; Sir Clifford Sifton helped in opening up the west and thus expanding the free trade area in Canada, and we entered upon a great period of development. That is the history-every time the world has moved out of depression it has been because trade has expanded and greater freedom has come to the people.
But what do we hear to-day? Prom various corners of this house, from all over the dominion we have other suggestions; let us try this; let us try that; let us have a little more currency; let us have a social dividend- whatever that means-let us have a just price; let us have some of the things which Premier Aberhart is promising to the people of Alberta anything except the thing which would make use free. Always and forever the human race seeks distant Pharpars and Abanas and will not take the remedy that lies at home. Under the government we have to-day we look forward to a movement in the right direction. We have made a start and are going forward. It is forward with Liberalism, freedom and progress, or backward to stagnation with the opposing forces.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been my privilege to listen to the budgets brought down from the time of the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding. I heard him bring his budgets down; he was followed by the Hon. Mr. Robb, the Hon. Mr. Dunning, the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, the Hon. Mr. Rhodes and again Mr. Dunning. I have yet to hear one budget that has carried with it the unanimous support and approval of all parties; in very commonplace language, "someone's ox had always to be gored."

The Budget-Mrs. Black (Yukon)
During the early part of this session we had the treaty between Canada and the United States. I did not want to vote against that treaty because I knew it was going to be of help to the Yukon. In the Yukon we import everything we use-our clothes, our food, our machinery. But in thinking the matter over, I felt conscientiously that I had to vote against that treaty because it affected the whole of Canada, and to explain my reason for voting against the treaty I must go back to the reciprocity agreement of 1911. During that campaign, when my husband was working very hard for the election of the hon. gentleman to my left (Mr. Stevens), I received from my father in the United States a letter written to him by an uncle of mine who at that time was president of one of the largest manufacturing concerns in that country. In that letter this uncle said, "There is an election campaign going on in Canada. It is for a reciprocity treaty, and we have stopped our building in Montreal. We are not, going ahead in Toronto. If the treaty goes through, all our manufacturing will be done in the United States." Naturally, therefore, I felt that this treaty would hurt the factories, the manufacturers of Canada, and that is the reason I voted against it. As I have said, the Yukon imports everything, and it exports what the world needs-gold, silver and a small quantity of other metals. I was pleased as a Yukoner when the treaty went through; as a Canadian I am still wondering.
During this session I have listened to speakers on all sides with reference to the railway question. First one speaker brings forward everything he can possibly think of against the Canadian National Railways. The Canadian National is the heaviest drain on the national resources, and the speaker will inveigh against carrying it on. A part of the press inveighs against the expenditures of the Canadian National system. On the other hand, speakers rise in the house and inveigh against the Canadian Pacific Railway, and a part of the press does the same. The Canadian Pacific is the heaviest taxpayer in Canada to-day. I have no brief for either railway, but at the same time it seems to me that as sensible men and women we should stop this continual sniping, first against one road and then against the other. As sensible people, as we value this country, as we value the future not only of ourselves but of our children and of our grandchildren, we should think of business first and of political sniping afterwards. I for one am sick of it.
I sometimes wonder how many people in this house or in the country would recognize 12739-172
the name of Onderdonk, one of the greatest railway builders Canada lias ever known. In the early nineties I knew that man as inti mately as any family friend; he was very much at home in my father's house in Chicago. I heard him tell tales of romance, hard work and the investment of capital in the building of the Canadian Pacific railway in the west, how those men blasted their way through the fearful mountain ranges. Others will say: But the government gave the Canadian Pacific a kingdom. Well, maybe the government of that day did give something to the Canadian Pacific Railway. But who wanted that kingdom at that time? When the United States bought Alaska, why did not Canada, why did not Great Britain buy it at the time for the paltry sum of $7,200,000? Because no one wanted it; and afterwards we say that we have done this and done that. Let us have some sense.
The Minister of Finance, to bring down a budget that would please everybody, would have to be a magician, a hypnotist and a prestidigitator all in one. I have never yet heard of that man in any country in the world. The sales tax will hit the Yukon quite a bit but I am hoping the treaty will offset that. The Yukon, as I said in very few words a short time ago, suffers some injustices from the federal government. Consider those civil servants who for years paid into the superannuation fund on both salary and living allowance. Some on retiring received from the fund the amounts which they had paid in. Suddenly the government, seemingly for no reason whatever, changed the order; retiring civil servants were told that they would be paid only on their salaries. The money paid into the fund on living allowance was refunded or an order was made that it should be. This was a most unjust, and, to me, an absolutely dishonest ruling. It is just as though one of you gentlemen had paid for life insurance amounting to $5,000 or $10,000. You paid your premiums year in and year out and you died. Your wife and family went to the insurance company to collect the insurance and were told by the officials, "Yes, true; we are sorry. Your husband did pay the premiums but we have decided that we can hardly afford to pay you the $5,000 or $10,000, so we will give you half." I have been told that the government should never have made this promise. I am not disputing that, but the government did make the promise. When a man retires, too old to take out other insurance, too old perhaps to work, why should he then be cheated in connection with what he has paid in?
As regards the Yukon-and I may say it is about all I know in this world-one heavy

2696	COMMONS
The Budget-Mrs. Black (Yukon)
charge that is made against us is on account of the telegraph line through northern British Columbia. I would suggest that the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Hanson) try to get the government to put part of that charge on his constituency because it certainly is not fair that the Yukon should be charged with an amount of money which is spent in British Columbia.
Our government in the Yukon consists of a commissioner and council of three members, elected one from the Whitehorse district, one from the Dawson district and one from the Mayo district. I do not believe that in any place in Canada to-day is a more honest effort made by any government in power to spend every dollar to the greatest advantage. Our crying need is always roads, and yet more roads. This year the government in power has seen fit to be more generous to the Yukon, and the mining industry, which is the backbone of our life there, will benefit by that generosity.
In the early days of the Yukon mining was carried on largely by individuals, but in a few years that was changed. Huge grants of land were given to political favourites. One mining recorder walked from Daw'son to The Porks at night and reported to the government at Ottawa that the tract of land over which he had walked in a few hours was not fit for individual mining, and these huge concessions were given to pampered favourites. The Klondike concession, forty miles of the Klondike river from rim to rim, the richest country in the Yukon, was originally given outright. The concession has changed hands from time to time until finally it is now owned by the Yukon Consolidated Gold Corporation Limited. That company has put up hundreds of thousands, nay millions of dollars, but owing to dishonest, corrupt or incompetent managers, it has always been in the red. It has changed its managership within the last year. During the recent campaign, in every small public meeting I held, I did not hesitate to say that the bunk houses furnished by this company for its men were not fit habitations for a well-bred dog. I am told that this company is now putting up, notwithstanding its failures in the past, another two million dollars this year. It is putting this money into new dredges; it is adding to its hydraulic machinery; it is digging new ditches, and there are also to be new camps for its men. I had letters recently saying that some of these bunk houses, the new ones, are well built, with large rooms, but as yet no accommodation for bathing, showers or anything of that sort has been provided for the men. This is not quite fair.

Then, too, our work in that country is practically all seasonal; when the men sign on they sign on for eight hours, ten hours, or even twelve hours a day, and when these men sign on for the summer work for ten or twelve hours a day they must sign a paper saying that they will work for twenty-five cents an hour for any extra hours. That is not just. Someone may say: But why do they sign on then; why do that work? Well, I would say to you men here: If you had a wife and family or if you had no other way of living than by taking that work you would certainly take it if you were honest and decent and preferred to work rather than be on relief. The men work so hard during the summer of five, six or seven, and in very rare cases eight months, that they become almost automatons. They are worn out; they are weary; they are dragged, and they have little at the end of those eight months to show for the work they have done. One may say that they need not sign on, but they must sign on if they would do anything.
Then, again it is said that living up there is so much cheaper. Well, living is cheaper than it was in the early days when we had to pay $1 a pound for sugar and S3 a pound for butter, and everything else accordingly. Now, while living is cheaper, bread still costs twenty-five cents a loaf. In the summer when the fresh fruit comes in, watermelons are $3 apiece; honeydews or muekmelons-and we seldom get a muskmelon-are from SI .50 to $250. Chickens the year round run from $2.25 to $3.50 each, depending upon the size of the bird and the time of year. During the summer in the north we pay S18 a cord for wood, $10 a month for water for the house and garden, and $10 a month for our telephone.
So it does not seem to me that any reasonably minded man should hesitate if we could pass a minimum wage law in that north country providing for, say $4.50 a day for an eight hour day, with board, and for the extra hours accordingly. The past government tried to put through $1.25 for the regular hours. We have an eight hour law in the Yukon, but the government official who drafted that law' is also an official and director of this mining company. I must say that the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) gave me an interview the other day and said that he would carefully consider this matter of the eight hour law in the north. At the present time the price of gold is twice what it was when the company first commenced work and had to

The Budget-Mr. Elliott (Kindersley)
work under much more difficult circumstances than now.
We in the north are anxious to do what we can. I do not think we complain. We want to do the best we can not only for the north but for Canada as a whole. I think in my thirty-eight years of living in that north country I could count on the fingers of one hand the men who preferred loafing to working-yes, and then I would have several fingers left.
Under no circumstances do I wish to be unfair or to put an unnecessary handicap on industry. I want to be fair to the men who elected me. They were the labouring men of the Yukon. I want to be just as fair to the company which did everything in its power to prevent my election, because I understand perfectly well that no matter where we are, labour needs capital and capital needs loyal labour, and if capital and labour are always ready to spring at each other's throats the rest of us are hurt and the world is hurt.
The Yukon is pleased to learn that the topographical and mining surveys are to be continued this coming summer. I would only like to be allowed to suggest to the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Crerar) that his deputy consider putting on these mining surveys some of our own boys in that north country.
I was elected as Yukon's representative by the combined vote of stand-pat Conservatives, friends of thirty odd years standing, and as well by the support of a number of genuine Liberals who were certainly not well treated by the representatives of their party in British Columbia and the Yukon. The Yukon is an enormous territory with great potentialities, and I would like to feel that the two ministers in the government who are most interested in that territory, the hon. Minister of Labour and the hon. Minister of the Interior, would visit us. They would receive the warmest kind of welcome. A few years ago it would have taken them weeks, nay months to make the trip, but with present day flying conditions they could make the trip from Ottawa to Dawson and return, going by way of the Hudson bay if they so desired, in less than two weeks. They would see things at first hand and could understand better than ever our needs and necessities. While not always agreeing with the policies of the government, as I said before, I do wish to thank the ministers for what they have done this session to help the Yukon. Again I extend an invitation to the members of the government to visit us and to know at first hand what we need.
Mr. O'. B. ELLIOTT (Kindersley):	Mr. Speaker, I welcome the criticism of the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman), because I believe that any policy which cannot stand the criticism of this House of Commons is not worth advocating. I expect the minister will hear more in reply to the criticisms the hon. member has made. I wish to associate myself with hon. members who have extended congratulations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) upon the very impressive manner in which he presented his budget speech. I am sure that all those within hearing distance must have been impressed with the sincerity with which he delivered his speech. However, things were different when one was away from the influence of his great personality. Upon rereading his speech we then saw that there were some things lacking in the fulfilment of our desires. It takes a considerable amount of, I might say intestinal fortitude for a new member to attempt to criticize an important document of this kind, and in speaking this afternoon I speak more in the spirit of suggestion than in that of criticism.
Practically every thoughtful person must have given considerable study to the various systems by which we hope to realize our desires in obtaining a solution of the present difficulties in our economic system. Reviewing some of the assertions made by different ministers with regard to cooperation between th federal government and the various provincial governments, I found a piece of legislation passed by the Saskatchewan legislature. Bill No. 120, an act to amend the Local Improvement Districts Relief Act, is somewhat in fine with the principles that have been advocated. Section 2 reads as follows:
The minister may make advances by way of loan to settlers resident in local improvement districts or in rural municipalities for the purchase of food, clothing and building material, for medical and hospital care and treatment, for the purchase of work stock, milch cows, brood sows, poultry, feed, fodder' petroleum products, seed, machinery, implements, repairs to implements and parts and binder twine, for the payment of freight on settlers' effects, homestead entry fees, timber or hay permit fees and for improvements on crown lands and other lands, for the purpose of breaking land, the surveying of drainage of land for settlement purposes, and the moving and reestablishment on land of persons on relief or about to become public charges.
The only difficulty in connection with this bill is to be found in section 1, which reads as follows:
Subsection 1 of section 5 of the Local Improvement Districts Relief Act, as amended by section 4 of chapter 38 of the statutes of 1934-35, is further amended by striking out

Subsection 2 of section 2 reads:

It seems to me that our financial system is always trying to saddle our people with the maximum load of interest they can bear instead of making a minimum rate, which is the most desirable. In Saskatchewan the rural population is 79-7 per cent of the whole and the welfare of the whole province is vitally dependent upon the success of the farmers. During the last five years the equilibrium of the province has been upset because of financial conditions which have compelled many farmers to seek avenues of revenue besides the farm. Many of them have gone to the towns to open up business ventures of various kinds. Most horn, members are familiar with the law of diminishing returns. A town with a given population can support only a given number of business places. Many of these farmers have opened up stores, trucking concerns, garages and other places of business, and the result has been disastrous to many of the old established places. Many of these old firms had extended credit to farmers during the difficult days of crop failures and they were forced to compete with new ventures which were opened up debt free and carried on mostly on a cash basis. The result was that many of the older firms eventually went into bankruptcy.
It seems to me that Canada is making exactly the same error in connection with our transportation system. We built thousands of miles of railway lines and then we proceeded to construct highways practically parallel to the railway lines to serve a population which was not increasing at the same ratio as we increased our transportation facilities. The trucking business is not sufficiently well controlled, as far as financing is concerned, and it is not compelled to abide by any fixed charges.

speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock I was saying that the trucking business is not sufficiently well controlled to compel the operators to abide 
by any fixed charges. I know of many cases during the last few years where small truckers have gone into that business to provide themselves with some means of sustenance. They found the rates charged by going to the railway station and obtaining the classification and rates on freight between given points, and then, in order to obtain business, they transported their goods at a smaller charge. In addition to this we are also providing assistance to all manner of shipping, both foreign and local, through a free canal system. When hon. members consider that the Canadian National Railways spent during 1935 about $24,000,000 on their right of way, they will agree that it is hardly consistent with good business to provide free means of transportation for other systems. We have in Canada 509-4 miles of canals, giving us 1,846 miles of waterways open to navigation. Since the commencement of the building of canals, Canada has spent $336,564,618, on which revenues of $30,851,699 have been received, $14,000,000 of this being between 1868 and 1910, in which latter year canal tolls were cancelled. The estimates this year show that we are about to spend many more millions on harbours and canals.
Records shows that in 1934, 22,217 Canadian and 2,044 United States vessels, with a registered total of 17,736,818 tons, used our canals. Freight carried was as follows: Canadian, 10,813,922 tons, or 59-8 per cent; United States, 7,255,330 tons, or 40-2 per cent: passengers handled were 69.990. The 1935 returns show a total of 25,694 vessels, with a tonnage of 18,204,468 tons, or an increase of 135,216 tons. If hon. members will compare this with the revenue freight handled by the railways, it will be observed that on the Canadian National Railways the revenue tonnage was 38,807,718 tons, and on the Canadian Pacific railway, 26,094,183 tons, or a total of 64,910,901 tons, so that the canal handled almost 30 per cent of the total revenue tonnage. In addition to this, people in their criticism fail to make note of the thousands of tons of freight, both carload and less than carload, that have been handled free during the last few years of depression, and I might say that the people in my constituency who have received quite a large part of this relief appreciate the services of the railways.
I wish to place on record comparisons of the traffic between the ports to indicate the service given by our canal system: Between Canadian ports, upstream, 4,063,850 tons; down, 6,119,551 tons; Canadian to United States ports, 1,895,272 tons up, and 197,614 tons down; between United States ports, up, 398,815 tons; down, 551,523 tons; United States to Canadian ports, up, 162,102 tons;

The Budget-Mr. Elliott (Kindersley)
down, 4,680,625 tons. During the season of navigation 140 cargoes, or 211,169 tons of freight, passed up the St. Lawrence canal from Europe and north American Atlantic ports. This included 22,704 tons of anthracite coal, all for Toronto, from England-and this, it may be observed, was in competition with our Canadian coal-56,058 tons of wood pulp, almost entirely for United States ports, from Norway, Sweden, Germany, Est'honia, and the maritime provinces; 61,372 tons of pulp wood for Thorold and Oswego area and other United States ports, all but one cargo being from the maritime provinces. A great deal of this freight was handled by Norwegian tramps in competition with our own vessels. In 1935 wood pulp carried on the St. Lawrence amounted to 380,876 tons, and pulp wood, to 619,907 tons, and a large amount of hard and soft coal was transported as well. During the present year, from April 24 to May 8, 148 Canadian, two American, and seven foreign boats, principally Norwegian, were engaged in handling wood pulp, china clay and merchandise.
I note also that, according to the Montreal Star of May 7, three more Norwegian tramps have cleared their ports with sulphite pulp billed to Montreal. On May 5 the Montreal Star states:
More tramps have been chartered to go to the head of the lakes and take grain from there to Europe. Lake ship owners are anything but pleased, for they say they have plenty of ships available. One lake ship man bitterly complained yesterday that wages were about one-third on the Norwegian tramps what they were on Canadian ships. Canada has plenty of lake ships, but cannot compete against the Norwegian tramps on toll free canals, he complained.
Among those going up to take Canadian grain at the head of the lakes are Audun, Koinet, Lab, Rondo, Bette, Bonde, Ornefjell, and Asgerd.
The Norwegian tramp, Margit R., which passed up the canal for the lakes, was the first ship to go by this year with her boilers on deck. She had a load of coal from Swansea to Toronto.
In the Star of May 6 I find the following
criticism:
An equally menacing form of competition to Canadian railways is to be found in subsidized waterways. Operators on these, who at one time were primarily occupied in moving bulk products, are increasingly encroaching on package and other freight. It is hoped that the government will give active consideration to plans for making inland waterways selfsupporting. The development of the methods of transportation which compete with rail services has been very largely the result of large public expenditures made without any real consideration of the economic consequences. The railways are naturally interested in corrective measures, but it should not be
forgotten that the interest of the taxpayers in the sound financial policies of public authorities is even more pressing....
All railways on this continent are being subjected to increasing competition from highway transport. It cannot be doubted that the motor vehicle has a permanent place in our economy, but it is equally true that the railroad has not been supplanted as the most important element in the transport field. It would appear that the proper function of the motor vehicle is to serve as a supplement to, rather than a substitute for, railroads. _
Highway transportation of freight, in its present form, has suffered from acute internal competition and cannot be regarded generally as a proven economic enterprise.
Canadian railways have also lost a considerable amount of traffic through the Panama canal. Of 2,201,180 tons of Canadian traffic originating on the west coast, 498,708 tons were destined to Canada's east coast; of 196,204 tons originating on Canada's east coast 189,227 tons were destined to Canada's west coast. The report of the governor of the Panama canal zone for the year ended June 30. 1934, reveals that 5,553 vessels, with 28,566,595 canal net tonnage, passed through the canal, and the tolls collected amounted to $24,063,789. It seems to me that toll charges Dn a similar ratio on the Canadian canals would provide a return of possibly $18,000,000 or $20,000,000.
There is no doubt that the solution of our railway problem is increased business, and I believe also that there should be a department of transport possibly along the lines set out in the resolution which is No. 28 on the order paper, and which states:
That it is expedient to provide for a department of transport to comprise the present Department of Railways and Canals-
The greatest deterrent to the business of Canada, of course, is not only the heavy taxation in the municipalities, cities and towns, but also the indirect taxation. As far as our housing scheme is concerned, it is impossible for the great majority of our people to build houses with money at five per cent and taxes at their present rate. If we take into consideration the income tax returns for 1934 we shall readily see the impossibility of a large number of Canadians ever owning their own homes. The income tax returns show that in Canada in 1934, 390 persons received $100,000 or more; 1,853 persons received between $25,000 and $100,000 ; 28,896 persons received from $5,000 to $25,000 ; 246,057 received between $1,000 and $5,000, and 3,765,971 had incomes of $1,000 or less.
We should take a lesson from the past; the enormous interest and tax burden that we have attempted to meet could be explained by the national policy introduced by Sir John A.
2700	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Elliott (Kindersley)
Macdonald in 1873. In its essentials that policy was based upon a protective tariff and sound money. It has been demonstrated that it was based also upon the mistaken idea that the individual Canadian must spend a lifetime working for the system built up under the national policy, and must be content to accept in return whatever may be left after all other demands have been met. It may be said that it is one thing to make this broad statement and another thing to prove it, but this is the experience of the last fifty-six years: In 1936 the population of Canada only slightly exceeds the population of 1879. In the interval Canada has absorbed some 3,000,000 people from Europe, who have displaced or replaced young Canadians who have moved to the United States, where the Canadian population is said to exceed 15,000,000. In the fifty-six years to which I have referred the existing public utilities and fixed assets of Canada, including the railways, have been put into place on such terms and conditions that Canada owes more than the entire cost of construction, and more than the replacement value. The weakness of our present system is that it maintains poverty as a necessary and recognized institution, and seeks to carry a religion of faith and idealism on the backs of the people who are oppressed by material necessities and human ills.
This is only another way of saying that the system has always insisted upon maintaining poverty in the midst of plenty, dividing the people into rich and poor, enforcing the rights of property by power of law, and restricting human rights to every extent necessary to keep money sound. An individual cannot eat ethics, and in all sincerity I say that there should be credited and devoted to the factor of restoration in Canada a fully adequate share of the credit and money of the nation. There must be a restoration, by immediate remedial action, of an adequate Canadian standard of living. Nothing less and nothing else will satisfy the electors of Canada. This country can be made the richest nation, per individual of population, in the world; the assets exist but are locked up most securely.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended taking part in this debate, but in view of the fact that I seconded the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), I feel that I ought to make a few observations with regard to the salient points of the budget.
May I begin, like others who have preceded me, by complimenting the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) upon the comprehensive manner in which he presented his budget, and 
on the earnest and sincere way in which he approached this great problem.
First of all I should like to mention some of the features in this budget that seem commendable to me, coming as I do from an agricultural constituency in western Canada. The reduction in the intermediate tariff rate on gasoline and distillate, if it is reflected in a reduced price to the consumer, will be of great benefit to western farmers, particularly in those areas where they are largely machine farmers. There gasoline and distillates enter into the production of their crops. Covering large areas, as they do, this is part of their cost of transportation, and a large part of their income is used up in buying gasoline and distillate. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, if this reduction in the tariff rate is reflected in a reduced price, as we hope it will be, we feel that the Minister of Finance is to be congratulated upon having taken this step.
We believe also that the $100 worth of goods which may be brought into this country by tourists is a commendable feature. I do not feel that I want to take advantage of this provision; I have always felt that one ought to spend his money where he earned it, but while I would not want to take full advantage of this offer the fact remains that because of the times in which we live thousands of people are compelled to make their dollar go as far as possible. There has been a concerted demand, particularly from along the boundary, that the privilege now enjoyed by residents of the United States should be extended to Canadian tourists, and I feel that in taking tihis step the Minister of Finance has done something which will be in the best interests of our people.
I think, too, that the increase in the corporation tax to fifteen per cent is a move in the right direction. In the United States for some time past they have had a corporation tax of sixteen per cent, so a fifteen per cent tax is not at all out of proportion. It is only right that those who have made large profits out of the society in which they live, and have been able to make them only because of the existence of the society, should pay a fair share towards the maintenance of that society.
But most of all is the minister to be congratulated upon the lowering of the tariff on farm implements. The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lawson) said the other evening that while we of agricultural constituencies might be glad, he. thinking of the workers, was not at all happy about this. I would point out that never to my knowledge has a protected industry been an industry which has looked after the workers. In fact it is

The Budget-Mr. Douglas
commonly said that protected industries have been the most sweated industries and those in which wages are lowest. We, too, are interested in the workers, but I hardly think that the worker will be helped very much by high tariffs on farm implements. But if lowering the tariff on farm implements means a lower price to the farmer, this will be of great material benefit. I say "if"; it has not always been the case. I have in my hand a report of the Searle Grain Company dated Thursday, March 19, 1936, in which they list ten farm implements. I am going

This reveals the fact, that to-day one would have to spend three bushels of wheat to buy the same amount of farm machinery that in 1913 could have been purchased for one bushel of wheat. It shows .that tihe cost of farm implements had increased out of all proportion to that of the other commodities the farmer has to buy either to produce or to live. But the most significant fact is that out of the ten items I have listed seven have increased in price since last year. We heard a great deal during the general election that if only we could get a lower tariff on farm implements the cost to the farmer would come down; yet the fact is that of the ten listed seven are higher this year than last. Therefore in the west we are apprehensive. We are hoping, and I think the Minister of Finance is hoping, that this decrease of five per cent in the tariff on farm implements will mean a decrease in price. If it does he is to be congratulated. I am not going to say any more about this because a committee has been set up to investigate the matter and I do not wish to anticipate its findings, but if this reduction in tariff is not followed by a reduction iD price there will be great disappointment among the agricultural producers of western Canada.
I am very glad to be able to congratulate the Minister of Finance upon these things: the lowered rate on gasoline, the increased corporation tax, the permission to bring back $100 of goods free of duty, the lower tariff on farm implements. Sometimes hon. gentlemen opposite have taken the attitude that we in this group delight to find fault. That is not true; we are only too glad to congratulate any minister upon a fine piece of work. When we criticize, as I must now proceed to do, it is not because we love the Minister of Finance less but because we love Canada more.
I shall confine my remarks particularly to the first part of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis):
This house regrets that the proposals submitted by the Minister of Finance on May 1 are entirely inadequate to meet the acute and serious situation prevailing in Canada.
I was interested to find that those words are exactly the amendment which was moved last year by an hon. gentleman who is now of the government party. I felt that conditions had ohanged so little since last year, that this amendment was still very much in order. There are in the budget two things particularly which do not commend themselves to me: first, the inequality in the raising of the national revenue, and, second, the inequality in the expenditure of it.
As to the inequality in the raising of the national revenue, one would naturally have expected that since the country is facing a large deficit there would have been a substantial increase in the income tax in the higher brackets. But such was not the case. Lest some might think that, perhaps, there are no higher brackets of any consequence, I have in my hand figures of the incomes assessed for income war tax in Canada, in 1934. The Budget-Mr. Douglas

to be divided among the other sixty per cent of the people. This means that those who are receiving large incomes have, in relation to what they receive, very little taken from their average purchasing power by the tax. Two things, it seems to me, ought to be done. First, the names of these people and the amounts on which they pay income tax should be published. We ought not to wonder that suspicion is rampant. We cannot wonder that people misunderstand, when the governments hesitates to print the names and amounts received by these individuals. The other thing is that without hurting these people very seriously, we could grade steeply the income tax, not only in steps of $5,000, but every $1,000, so that each $1,000 might pay proportionately higher than the preceding $1,000. One would have expected this to be done, but it was not. The Minister of Finance spoke quite longingly about Great Britain; yet we know that to-day Great Britain has very steeply graded her income tax, with the result that in some of the highest brackets as much as fourteen shillings in the pound is taken. But no such step has been taken in this budget.
Then we suggested that a levy might be taken on wealth.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Before my hon. friend leaves the income tax, would he permit a question? In making comparisons with Great Britain, has my hon. friend added to the federal income tax in Canada the provincial income taxes now prevailing? There is in Great Britain only one income tax whereas in Canada there are two and sometimes three.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No. I have not added the provincial income tax; but the fact remains that the provincial income tax, like the federal, does not emphasize the higher brackets. It is the people in the lower brackets, and not those in the higher brackets who pay the major part of the national revenue.
The second thing we suggested was a levy on wealth and undivided profits. The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) said that he could not support our proposal because it was a move in the direction of socialism, and yet he proceeded to suggest a reduction in interest rates on bonds, which really would have the same effect but would not distribute the burden as equally. To cut interest on bonds indiscriminately-and we are in agreement with a reduction in interest rates-would strike not only at the large financier but at those people who are dependent for their livelihood upon small groups of shares, life insurance policies, annuities and so on. But by levying a tax on wealth you 
would take from those who have and who can best afford to contribute revenue towards the support of the country. Let me take an example. On page 52 of the price spreads report I find that the Imperial Tobacco Company and subsidiaries showed, from 1929 to 1933, undivided profits amounting to $11,886,573. On page 115 I find that the Macdonald Tobacco Company at the end of 1933 had undivided profits amounting to $594,432, despite the fact that the president had taken out $260,000 annually since 1930. These are two instances. Surely they are not isolated; surely there are in Canada other accumulations of similar undivided profits. Surely, therefore, these are places to which we ought to go in all fairness to gather some of the revenue by which to finance the dominion. It was suggested this afternoon that this is a socialist measure; yet it was tried in Germany by the government there, not socialist, on two different occasions to meet financial crises. I would not vouch for the authenticity of this, but it has been estimated that by a levy on wealth in . Canada, spread over a period of five years, it would be possible to get somewhere in the neighbourhood of $2,000,000,000. I suggest that that is worthy of serious consideration.
We suggest further that some revenue might be raised by inheritance taxes. In Great Britain to-day when men are leaving behind them large fortunes to their next of kin the state feels that in view of the fact that they made those fortunes within the country and by the aid of all the people in the country, the people of that country have a right to some share of those fortunes. This would be a good place to work out what the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) suggested. He spoke of our cultural heritage; he said that we have this and we have that. I could not help wondering whom he meant by "we"; a good many people are not included in that "we," for a good many people have not much of an inheritance. It is true that there are books and all the other fine contributions to our cultural heritage, but they are not procurable by thousands of people, and these things might be made available to these people through the collection of inheritance taxes on fortunes passed on from generation to generation. In Great Britain to-day by the time a fortune has passed through the exchequer, one-third has been taken for government revenue. But this government did not see fit to raise money in any one of these ways; rather, it chose to raise money largely by increasing the sales tax from six to eight per cent.

The Budget-Mr. Douglas

There can be no more pernicious form of taxation than the sales tax. I will not go into the details of it, but there are three facts to be pointed out in connection with it. In the first place, it takes from the consuming power of the great mass of consumers; the average man, in other words, will have two per cent less to buy goods with; there wall be two per cent less for the storekeeper, and two per cent less going into circulation. I remember seeing last year large bill-boards showing a man tied up with ropes, and there was this inscription, "Let him free; vote Liberal." Yet here we are tying up internal trade in the most effective way possible by taking two percent more from the pockets of the people. But there is something else. Like the sugar tax, the sales tax affects largely those who have the biggest families and who have to buy the basic necessities of life. When people have to buy sugar for five or six or seven children they pay five or six times as much under the tax, whereas people who do not spend their money on basic commodities pay less. We all remember one of the axioms in the economic text-books, called Jevin's Criteria, where it is pointed out that the smaller the income the larger the proportion that goes for basic necessities, whereas, in the case of larger incomes, more goes in investments, education and in other directions. Consequently the major part of the sales tax will have to be borne by people who can least afford to pay it. The old couple with their $20 a month old age pension, buying a few groceries-

I am quite well aware of that, but the minister is stepping aside from the point. Industry uses machinery and it will cost industry more to produce certain articles; consequently the tax will be passed back in the price charged to the consumer. Whether we realize it or not, the consumer will pay indirectly. He will pay in the long run, and it is those who have to buy these commodities who will have to pas' the large share of the sales tax. It seems to me that this budget will give us confidence, if possible, at the cost of human security. As one reads the budget one feels that the minister or the government evidently believes that "for whosoever hath, to him shall be given; and whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken even that which he seemeth to have."
May I say a word now about the amendment to the amendment moved this afternoon. We in this group feel that we can agree with the amendment to the amendment inasmuch as it is couched in general terms, indicating very generally the desire to have consumption brought into line with production. But we cannot vote for this subamendment because it is moved in substitution for the amendment we now have, and to vote for it would be automatically to support the sales tax which we have condemned in our own amendment. We feel that perhaps the most pernicious thing in the entire budget is the levying of the sales tax, which has been increased by 33J per cent, and that to vote for this subamendment, agreeing with it as we do in general terms, would be to vote in favour of the sales tax, to which we are opposed whether it be levied by a provincial or federal government.
I should like now to turn attention to the inequalities in expending the national revenue. The main item of expenditure in the budget is the interest on the national debt of $3,432,000,000, an interest charge of $134,550,000, or 36 per cent of the budget. When we add to that the share of the Canadian National Railway deficit which the government pays, $47,000,000, that accounts for another 12 per cent of the budget, and with the loans which will be made to provincial governments to help clear up debts it will be seen that nearly fifty cents on every dollar of this budget is going to pay interest charges in one form or another. Now I would ask the government a question, the same question they have been asking us ever since this session started: V/here is the money coming from? Almost $200,000,000 goes to pay in-
The Budget-Mr. Douglas

terest charges in one form or another. That is to say, 62 per cent of the entire budget goes to pay fixed charges. Where are you going to get the money?

All right. After all,
capital is merely wealth used to produce more wealth, so it is merely quibbling over terms. Surely the minister will not deny that capital is wealth used to produce more wealth. We would place a levy on wealth. It might be liquid wealth, or merely frozen assets, and it could be paid over a period of time either in cash or in the form of securities.
Let me return to my question:	Where is
the money coming from? That is the question the minister asks us every time we propose anything. Here is $200,000,000 required to pay interest charges. Where are you going to get the money? Of course, we know where. The money will come from the revenues of the country. In other words, this is a fixed charge; it is something that must be paid. But the other 38 per cent

of the budget is not composed of fixed items. In other words, social services are not to be recognized as uncontrollable items of expenditure in the budget; only these interest charges are to be so regarded.
Let us consider our sense of values for a moment. The interest that we have to pay on our funded lebt accounts for 36 per cent of the total budget. Unemployment relief last year took $49,469,000 in round figures, or 13 per cent of the total; the Canadian National Railway deficit, $47,400,000, or 12 per cent of the total; the amount paid on wheat and oats, $6,770,000, or 1-5 per cent of the total; the amount paid out by the farm loan board, $7,933,000, or 1-6 per cent of the total; old age pensions, 4-5 per cent of the total; public works, $80,000,000, or 20 per cent of the total. In other words, if we add the amounts for unemployment relief, Canadian National Railway deficit, wheat and oats, we are still paying less for all that than we pay in interest charges on our funded debt.

speechtext:
I have only forty minutes, and it is passing very quickly.
Turning to our expenditure, we find in the estimates, in round figures, $13,377,000 for national defence; $4,130,000 for the air force; and in the supplementary estimates $5,317,000 for national defence, making a grand total, in round figures, of $22,825,000, or an increase over 1935-36 of $1,284,000. That is what we are spending on military estimates and national defence. We are spending on our legation at Geneva $614,890, a decrease of $10,502 from last year. In other words, Mr. Speaker, we are spending over forty times as much for war preparations as we are in the interests of peace.
We do not expect the minister to find the money growing on gooseberry bushes. We know he has a limited amount of money to spend, and there are a great many demands upon him, but we submit that pensions for the blind, an extension of the old age pension, some type of health policy, and legislation to take care of those who are crippled and incapacitated, are all items which ought to have a place in the list of expenditures. When it comes to finding money for these things the reply is: We have not the money. But when it comes to finding the money for interest charges-that is a fixed charge.

The Budget-Mr. Douglas
What is the government's policy as revealed by the budget? I think I am right in saying it is three things: Extension of external trade, a balanced budget, and protecting the credit of Canada. The Minister of Finance said that our external trade had increased by ten per cent, but at the same time he said, as reported on page 2363 of Hansard:
One of the most disappointing features of the business improvement so far is that the numbers of those on relief do not decline at the same pace as business activity recovers.
I think the government will come very slowly to the position to which we have come, that even with return of normal business activity we shall not have a return of prosperity, and a return to the former volume of trade and business activity will not mean the wiping out of unemployment or the solving of our economic difficulties.
The second feature which the minister stresses is a balanced budget. That can mean only one thing. There can be no cutting down on the fixed charges representing 62 per cent of the budget, and so it means that any cutting down must be on the other 38 per cent, unless we are prepared to tax these bondholders or cut the interest or principal of their bonds. Then a balanced budget must mean the cutting down of relief, pensions or some other type of social services. I wish to submit that wherever that has been attempted it has been a failure. It has meant higher taxes, fewer social services and a lower standard of living for the great masses of the people.
The other suggestion is that we shall protect the credit of Canada. What we mean when we talk about protecting credit is that we shall prevent any type of inflation which would hurt the creditor and help the debtor. Deflation has always been in the best interests of the creditor; inflation has always hurt the creditor. The Minister of Finance shakes his head, and yet is it not true that the creditor who has invested his money when money was cheap, and then experiences a period of deflation such as we have had in the last five years, finds that the return he gets from his money is a return in a dollar which will buy two or three times as much as the dollar he invested? Consequently a period of deflation is a paradise for him, but it is very different for the debtor who must pay back. Therefore, when we talk about protecting credit we really mean we intend to prevent anything which might upset the present state of deflation. In this corner of the house we are not inflationists, but neither are we deflationists. We have advocated managed currency, namely that currency and credit should be issued in proportion to goods.
In Germany there was a state of true inflation; she issued money which was valueless. Why? Because that money had nothing behind it. She did not produce goods in proportion to her money, so her money was worthless. In Canada we have done the opposite. We produce goods in abundance, but we have not produced sufficient money in proportion to purchase those goods, and the result is that we have deflation. Money without goods back of it is bad, but goods without money to purchase them is just as bad. It can be only by the issue of currency and credit in proportion to the goods issued that we can hope to establish a managed currency which will give the people purchasing power to consume the goods which they themselves have created.
A few days ago the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) said that he did not mind going forward, but he wanted to know where we were going. He believed in progress, but he said that he wanted ordered progress. I look over the budget, and I wonder whether the government knows where it is going. Is there any ordered progress? I look through public works expenditures placed here and there in a haphazard fashion, and I see no concerted financial policy.
It is true that during the election campaign hon. members such as the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer), the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) did enunciate some type of financial policy which might have been of value, but to date we have heard very little about it in the budget debate. As a matter of fact we have heard nothing constructive, and nothing to suggest that the government knows where it is going. Instead of that the tone of the budget and the demand of the minister on May 1 was: Back to May 1, 1930.
I submit that this is no time to go back. We can hardly expect a policy which brought us into this mess to pull us out of it. If a program could not prevent the greatest economic crisis in history, then it cannot hope to pull us out of it. Surely no hon. member thinks we can get out of the mire by tugging at our own shoelaces. This is not the time to tread beaten paths; it is time for the government to blaze new trails. The slogan of the government ought not to be: "Back to 1930"; it ought to be: "Forward, to greet the new day."
The Budget-Mr. Green

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, listening to the budget speech delivered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), and reviewing it with its various statements and tables as reported in Hansard one could not help being impressed with the seriousness of the problems facing Canada; neither could one fail to realize the burden being borne by the Minister of Finance, and for this reason, and also because he bears his burden with a smile, I cannot find it in my heart to deal harshly with his budget. I must say, however, that in many respects I dislike it; time alone will tell whether or not he has been wise, and in due course he will have to answer to the people of Canada for any mistakes. Meanwhile I wish to offer one or two suggestions in regard to the budget, and to place squarely before the house the question of aviation in Canada.
Dealing, first, with the budget, I would earnestly suggest that the minister reconsider the provision whereby goods valued at not more than $100 may be brought into the country free of duty by Canadian residents, after an absence of not less than forty-eight hours. Surely a provision such as that should apply only to travellers or tourists, and not to shoppers. If it is properly restricted there is some justification for the provision, although as all hon. members are aware, it will seriously affect the revenues of the dominion. I suggest, however, that the provision in its present form is simply an invitation to Canadian people living near the border to shop in the United States. As such it will seriously affect Canadian retail business and will set up one more magnet to draw our people to the south, instead of having them transact their business east and west in our own country.
Let me give as an illustration the situation in the city of Vancouver. The people on relief and those who are not fortunate enough to own a car, will have to buy their goods at home and probably at higher prices; they will have to pay a sales tax on most of the goods they need, which, by this budget, is increased from six per cent to eight per cent; in other words the poor people will get no help from the provision. On the other hand the man fortunate enough to own a car could quite justifiably get into his car in Vancouver on Friday night, after his day's business is concluded, drive to Bellingham or Seattle and return Sunday night, bringing with him, under this provision in the budget, groceries valued at $100; or if he chose he could bring back S100 worth of clothing; he could even go there and buy furniture on a time payment plan; for example, he could buy a vacuum cleaner valued at, say $90, making an initial

payment of $9 or $10 and agreeing to pay the balance under a hire-purchase agreement; and he can bring those goods back to Canada free of duty and free of sales tax. Surely the minister does not intend to have the provision go that far. If he does not, then I would suggest that the length of absence from Canada be extended beyond a period of forty-eight hours; that the exemption be cut from three times a year to twice a year; that a traveller be required to produce receipts showing that he has paid for the goods he is bringing back. Finally, I suggest that the exemption should be limited to purchases incidental to the trip, a provision which, I believe, appears in the United States tariff.
May 1 further suggest that the exemption be reduced from $100 to $35 or $50. It is so hard for us to remember that we have a population only one-twelfth that of the United States and to remember that most of our people are settled only 100 or 200 miles away from the border, which is not the case with the people of the United States. I do not think it is reasonable for us to expect to have everything the people in the United States can have, and to do everything that they can do. I suggest that if their exemption is to be $100 ours would be more than ample if it stood at $35 or $50.
I have this further suggestion in regard to the budget: I would ask that the minister reconsider the terms of the exemption from sales tax in connection with crushed stone or crushed gravel. At the present time the exemption reads as follows:
Crushed stone or crushed gravel to be used exclusively in the building or maintenance of provincial, county or township roads.
That leaves out cities and municipalities.

If they are going to have work done by a contractor they must pay that sales tax, and I do not see why there should not be an exemption for cities and municipalities. After all, in my province of British Columbia there exist no county organizations and no township organizations, which means that the exemption will apply only to provincial roads, whereas a great deal of the province is under municipal government; I suggest that in all fairness the municipalities and the cities

The Budget-Mr. Green
should get the benefit of the exemption. When the history of the last five years comes to be written it will be found that the municipal governments have borne more than their share of the burdens; they are bearing more than their share at the present time, and I do not think it is fair that they should be discriminated against in this w-ay.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Of course they are not, in fact.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Now I have a word of praise for the minister. I am pleased to see that he is trying to do away with uncertainty in mining taxation. The same principle of doing away with the uncertainty of government interference could well be applied to other industries of Canada, such as the farm implement industry, but as I do not represent an agricultural constituency I have nothing more to say as to that. However, as far as mining is concerned, no one can question that that industry has played a cheering part in the dark days through which this nation has just passed. The prospector, the miner, the engineer, the promoter, the financier, and all others engaged in mining have done much to raise the morale and the spirit of the Canadian people. I think we should accord them our admiration and our praise, and anything within reason that will assist them should meet with our approval. The industry has been greatly aided by aviation. Many of these mines would never have been developed but for aviation, and I suggest to the government that the time has now come when Canada should adopt a bold and aggressive air policy.
Let me tell the house in a few words the present position of civil aviation in Canada. I intend to treat the question in a nonpartisan spirit; it is a new problem and one which, in my opinion, should be dealt with in a non-partisan way. I wish that it were possible to discuss more of our difficulties in that way; we would get much further ahead.
First of all, let me give the house the bright side of this picture; that is, flying in northern Canada. I think it may fairly be said that flying has made possible Canada's great strides in gold mining and has advanced by decades the development of the northern section of our country. This is well set out in an article by Mr. J. A. Wilson, our own controller of civil aviation, to be found in the February issue of the Engineering Journal, from which I quote the following extract found at page 68:
The surveyor, geologist, and prospector were not slow to follow the example of the forester
and use aircraft as a better means of transportation and observation throughout the unsettled areas of Canada.
The result of this policy has been that to-day there exist generally throughout northern Canada efficient commercial air services which have been self-sustaining, have required no subsidy, and which give access to the remotest districts of the country. More has been learned of northern Canada during the past ten years than in the preceding three hundred. The forester, surveyor, geologist, prospector, mining engineer; the clergy, the doctors, the nurses, the police; in fact, all w-hose activities lie in northern Canada find their task greatly lightened, their range of action multiplied many times and their efficiency increased by the use of aircraft. Journeys which a few years ago meant weeks or months, and sometimes even years of toil and hardship, are now performed in ease and comfort in a few hours. The expansion of Canada's mining industry has greatly helped to tide Canada over the dark days of the depression and this development has been immensely assisted and hastened by aviation. Many of our most promising new mining fields owe their discovery and their opportunity of present development entirely to aircraft.
The figures of passengers, freight and mail carried by air in Canada during the last few years show the remarkable progress which has	been	made.	I	give the	approximate
figures: Passengers carried in 1933, 85,000; 1934, 105,000; 1935, 177,000-practically all in northern Canada. Freight carried, 1933,
4.205.000	pounds; 1934, 14,440,000 pounds; 1935,
26.439.000	pounds. It has almost doubled in the last year. Mail carried, 1933, 539,000 pounds; 1934, 625,000 pounds; 1935, 1,126,000 pounds.
Details of the air mail carried are given on	page	2146	of	Hansard.	The Postmaster General (Mr. Elliott, Middlesex) said, as reported on page 2140, that this mail was carried actually at a profit to the post office. All this development has been brought about by private enterprise, without subsidy of any kind from the government other than payment for	mail,	which,	as	I have remarked, wascarried at a profit to the post office. In addition to opening	up	northern	Canada, civil
aviation has been the means of training airmen who are without superior anywhere in the world. For instance, we have Hollick-Kenyon and Lymburner, two famous Canadian airmen whose exploits have not been properly recognized by this nation, two airmen who have done wonderful things in the last few months in the antarctic.. These men were trained through flying in northern Canada. I suggest that this is sound national develop-' ment for Canada. Our future is in the north. I believe that our destiny is to become a great northern nation, not a vest pocket edition of the United States of America.
The Budget-Mr. Green

I turn from the more pleasant side of the picture to aviation in the more thickly settled parts of Canada. What do we find? Quite a lot of flying has been done on fishery patrol on the coast of British Columbia. There are five mail routes, and five only, in the settled part of Canada, each one, with the exception of the route from Moncton to Charlottetown, being from Canada to the United States in order to get the mail down to the transAmerican airways. These five routes are to the south from Montreal, Winnipeg, Vancouver, and Victoria, and the one from Moncton to Charlottetown. So far as the trans-Canada airway is concerned, I understand it is hoped to complete the airway from Winnipeg to Vancouver in the summer of 1937.
